description: Powered entirely by cold pizza, blind optimism, and 48 hours without REM sleep, we are an unstoppable force of nature (and minor syntax errors). While the rest of humanity looks up at the stars and sees mysteries, we look up and see a lack of proper database indexing. If you combine our collective terminal history, you’d probably trigger a Homeland Security investigation or accidentally terraform Mars.
summary:
FieldShift Forecast gives Ontario farmers evidence-based crop rotation recommendations before they plant. It ranks rotations using real trial yields and shows where each number comes from.

We built an interactive tool for a Harrow, Ontario pilot. It combines cached NASA climate data (POWER, IMERG, GLDAS and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections to 2040), FAO crop suitability, soil data and real trial yields from the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada Harrow rotation trial.

Farmers can see which rotations held up best in the trial and how rain and temperature outlooks affect them. They can pick a crop and a target yield, replay the 2012 dry year, and browse other crops by suitability. Measured temperature at Harrow has risen about 0.75 °C per decade since 1981.

This answers the Field Shift challenge by turning NASA data into a planning aid for farm decisions as the climate changes. It matters because choosing a rotation is costly and hard to undo.

The scoring is transparent, not a black box. Every number shows its source and a label such as cached or derived. The tool compares historical trial evidence and does not predict yields.
details:
What it does

FieldShift Forecast helps an Ontario farmer compare crop rotations before planting. Our pilot is a cropland field near Harrow, Ontario. A map and a year slider (2021 to 2040) show climate from NASA data: observed up to 2025, then five NASA climate models. The dashboard ranks four corn, soybean and winter wheat rotations that have real Harrow trial yields. There are three views: Rotations (ranked options with their evidence), My crop (pick a crop and a bu/ac target and see whether each rotation meets it), and Other crops (suitability only, no invented bushels). It also replays any past season, including the 2012 drought, and shows the measured warming trend at the field: about 0.75 °C per decade since 1981.

How it works

All data is fetched once and cached, so the app never calls an outside service while running. Model 1 looks up FAO GAEZ crop suitability and checks growing-season rain (NASA POWER and IMERG) and soil pH. Model 2 is a transparent rule-based comparison. It divides each crop's trial yield by the best trial yield for that crop, averages per rotation, and shows gain over continuous cropping and gross revenue at dated Grain Farmers of Ontario prices. For corn only, we fitted Essex County yields against NASA weather and tested it on unseen years. We show where it was wrong (2012).

Impact and creativity

A wrong rotation costs a full season. FieldShift shows farmers evidence to compare options, not a guaranteed outcome. Every number carries a source and a label (CACHED, DERIVED, SAMPLE). It starts from the farmer's own crop and target, and it shows its own misses.

Limits we state openly

The trial site is about 26 km from the field, soil values are modelled, revenue is gross, and soil moisture is not projected.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, SQLite, Leaflet, JavaScript, pytest, Docker. Data: NASA POWER, IMERG, GLDAS, NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, FAO GAEZ, SoilGrids, AAFC Harrow trial. AI tools helped research and build; the team made all final decisions.
